title: Payment System
subtitle: Payment processing platform: idempotency keys, double-entry bookkeeping, PSP orchestration, and settlement reconciliation.
keyTakeaways: Enforce end-to-end idempotency at every layer: clients pass a unique Idempotency-Key locked atomically in the database (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING), and the Payment Executor passes a deterministic payment_order_id to external PSPs so retries never charge a card twice.

Record all financial movements in an immutable, append-only Double-Entry Ledger where every transaction writes at least two balanced entries (SUM(debits) == SUM(credits)): never use UPDATE account SET balance = balance - X as the primary ledger.

Never hold a database transaction open across an external network call to a payment gateway (Stripe/Adyen): persist state as EXECUTING first, call the PSP outside the database transaction, and update state via a Transactional Outbox.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A mission-critical Payment System accepts payments from customers, orchestrates transactions with third-party Payment Service Providers (PSPs), maintains an immutable financial ledger, and executes daily reconciliation.
bullets: Functional: Process one-time card and wallet payments; handle refunds and chargebacks; maintain an append-only double-entry financial ledger; run daily settlement reconciliation.
Functional: Multi-PSP routing (fallback to backup PSP if primary provider experiences downtime or degraded acceptance rates).
Non-Functional: Exactly-once payment semantics: a customer must never be charged twice for the same purchase under any failure condition.
Non-Functional: Strict regulatory compliance (PCI-DSS compliance: tokenize card data via hosted fields; never store raw PAN/CVV).
Out of Scope: Direct integration with central bank RTGS wire networks, foreign currency forex trading, and automated consumer credit scoring.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Payment platforms prioritize absolute data integrity, auditability, and deterministic recovery over raw volumetric throughput.
bullets: Transaction Volume: 10 million transactions per day (~120 payments/second average, peaking at 1,000 payments/second during promotions).
Ledger Write Volume: Each payment creates 4 to 6 ledger entries (customer debit, merchant credit, platform fee credit, processing fee debit). 10M payments = 50M ledger rows/day.
Latency Budget: End-to-end payment API latency < 2.5 seconds (p99), dominated by external card network round trips (typically 800ms to 1,500ms).
Availability Target: 99.999% availability for the payment ingestion layer, with zero data loss under regional failures.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Financial systems require modest storage capacity compared to media services, but require strict write durability and relational ACID guarantees.
bullets: Storage calculations: 50 million ledger rows/day * 200 bytes per row = 10 GB/day = 3.65 TB/year. A relational database cluster (PostgreSQL with streaming replicas) easily accommodates this volume.
Throughput sizing: 1,000 peak payments/sec = ~5,000 ledger writes/sec. This throughput is well within the capabilities of a tuned relational database primary using NVMe storage.
Audit archive: Encrypted cold storage (WORM S3 buckets) retained for 7 years to satisfy financial regulatory audit requirements.

codeSnippet.title: Payment System Capacity & Ledger Storage Worksheet
codeSnippet.code:
================================================================================
PAYMENT SYSTEM CAPACITY WORKSHEET (100M TXNS/DAY, 12,000 PEAK TPS)
================================================================================
1. THROUGHPUT & DATABASE IOPS
   - Avg Payment Write TPS    : 100,000,000 / 86,400        = 1,157 TPS
   - Peak Payment TPS (10x)   : 1,157 * 10                  = 11,570 TPS (~12K TPS)
   - Peak Ledger Row Inserts  : 12,000 TPS * 4 entries      = 48,000 inserts/sec
   - Peak Status/Dashboard QPS: 5,800 avg * 5               = 29,000 QPS

2. REDIS MEMORY (IDEMPOTENCY CACHE & DISTRIBUTED LOCKS)
   - 48h Idempotency Window   : 200,000,000 keys * 256 B    = 51.2 GB
   - Merchant Balance Cache   : 10,000,000 accts * 256 B    = 2.56 GB
   - Total Redis Cluster (2x) : (53.76 GB) * 2 (Replica)    = 107.5 GB RAM

3. 5-YEAR ACID DATABASE & LEDGER STORAGE
   - Per-Transaction Footprint: 2KB(Order) + 1KB(Ledger) + 2KB(Audit) = 5 KB
   - Daily Storage Growth     : 100M * 5 KB                 = 500 GB / day
   - 5-Year Raw Storage       : 500 GB * 365 * 5            = 912.5 TB
   - 3x Raft Replicated + Idx : 912.5 TB * 3 * 1.4          = 3.83 PB

4. NETWORK BANDWIDTH
   - Peak Control Plane I/O   : 42,000 QPS * 4 KB           = 168 MB/s (1.34 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Payment APIs require strong idempotency keys and stateful tracking across asynchronous processing stages.
bullets: Charge API: `POST /v1/payments/charge` takes `Header: Idempotency-Key: <UUID>` and body `{ orderId, amountCents, currency, paymentToken }`, returning `{ paymentId, status: "PENDING"|"CAPTURED"|"FAILED" }`.
Payment Orders Table: Stores `payment_id`, `idempotency_key`, `amount`, `status` (`INITIATED`, `EXECUTING`, `CAPTURED`, `FAILED`), and `psp_reference`.

Double-Entry Ledger Table: Stores `entry_id`, `transaction_id`, `account_id`, `direction` (`DEBIT` | `CREDIT`), `amount_cents`, and `timestamp`. Invariant: `SUM(debit) - SUM(credit) = 0` across every transaction.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The architecture decouples the synchronous API surface from external PSP network communications and post-processing ledger accounting.
bullets: Payment Gateway API: Validates card tokens, verifies client idempotency keys, and records pending payment orders.
Payment Executor: Executes external HTTP calls to PSPs (Stripe, Adyen) using deterministic merchant transaction IDs.
Double-Entry Ledger Service: Appends balanced debit and credit entries to the immutable ledger database.
Transactional Outbox & Event Publisher: Ensures database changes and Kafka events are published atomically.
Reconciliation Engine: Nightly batch service comparing internal ledger entries against settlement reports downloaded from PSPs and bank partners.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Executing payments safely requires decoupling database transactions from external network calls.
bullets: The external call anti-pattern: Never wrap an external PSP network call inside an open database transaction (`BEGIN; UPDATE ...; callStripe(); COMMIT;`). If Stripe takes 10 seconds to respond, database connection pools exhaust and cause a total system outage.

The 3-phase execution pattern: 1. Open DB transaction, insert payment order with status `EXECUTING`, commit immediately. 2. Make outbound HTTP call to PSP with timeout and retries. 3. Open second DB transaction, update status to `CAPTURED`, write ledger entries, commit.

Idempotency with external PSPs: Pass `payment_order_id` as the PSP's idempotency key. If network drops occur before receiving the PSP response, retrying with the same key guarantees the PSP returns the existing transaction status rather than charging the card again.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Financial platforms require automated reconciliation to detect and correct discrepancies between internal ledgers and third-party bank partners.
bullets: Reconciliation pipeline: At the end of each day (T+1), download bank settlement CSVs. Match every internal `CAPTURED` payment against the bank's cleared transaction reference. Flag missing, duplicate, or mismatched amounts for human investigation.
PSP health circuit breakers: Monitor PSP error rates and latency in real time. If Provider A error rates exceed 5%, automatically route new traffic to Provider B.

Cryptographic hash chains: Link ledger entries together using SHA-256 hash chains (`current_hash = SHA256(prev_hash + entry_data)`), ensuring any unauthorized tampering with historical financial records is immediately detected.

tradeOffs.pros: Complete auditability; mathematical guarantee of balance integrity; zero risk of lost updates.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher write volume (4-6 rows per payment); computing account balances requires summing historical entries or maintaining read projections.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Any platform handling real money, wallets, credit balances, or merchant payouts.

tradeOffs.option: Single Balance Mutation (UPDATE account SET balance = balance - X)
tradeOffs.pros: Simple to query; tiny database footprint.
tradeOffs.cons: Impossible to audit; vulnerable to race conditions; no historical record of why a balance changed.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Non-financial counters (e.g., video view counts, game score points).

tradeOffs.pros: Resilience against payment gateway outages; optimizes interchange fees across international currencies.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires maintaining multiple vendor integrations and normalizing webhook and reconciliation formats.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Global e-commerce platforms processing millions of dollars in monthly transactions.

interviewTip: Emphasize two core rules in payment system interviews: first, never hold a database transaction open while calling an external PSP over the network; second, always model money using an immutable double-entry ledger where debits equal credits, rather than updating a single balance column.
